title: Aerion's Quiet Dance
markdown:
Far above the slumbering world, where clouds drifted like fluffy sheep in a celestial meadow, lay the Archipelago of the Whispering Peaks. Colossal giants reaching for the stars, jagged tops piercing the sky. Spidery rope ferries of sturdy mountain moss swung across misty gulfs. In hidden valleys, bells chimed a melody on the wind.

In a cozy nook carved into Mount Glimmer lived Morwen, a witch brimming with skill and an even bigger dollop of curiosity. She was not one for cackling over cauldrons or potions that turned noses green. She was fascinated by the subtle shimmer of twilight, the secret whispers of moss, and the quiet triumph of a perfectly organized spice rack. Her constant companion was Bunting, a marmot with a calm spirit and a nose for the most delectable alpine berries. Fur the colour of sun-baked earth. Tiny paws expert at digging sweet roots. He often shared his treasures, a silent offering of woodland wisdom.

One crisp morning, the kind where the air tasted like mint tea served extra cold, a runner arrived, puffing, specked with mist, cloak damp, muddy footprints on Morwen’s polished floor.

“The elders. They plead with you. The Sky-Song Festival. You must judge.”

Morwen blinked, spectacles sliding. She nudged them back. “The Sky-Song Festival? The one with competitive cloud-sculpting and echo-dueling? I’ve always wondered if a perfectly timed yodel could win an echo contest, or if the clouds ever got tired of looking like sheep.”

“Precisely,” squeaked the runner. “And the dragon displays. The grandest event of the year. They say your judgment is as sharp as a hawk’s.”

Morwen, slightly puzzled by competitive dragon-flying—she had only ever seen them politely circling for stray sheep, looking rather bored—found herself intrigued. So many creatures, unique talents. Wonder, tickled.

“Very well. Inform the elders that Morwen of Mount Glimmer will be there. And Bunting, of course. He has an excellent ear for harmonious churring.”

Bunting churred, whiskers twitching, already imagining roasted nuts, the faint metallic tang of dragon breath, the sweet perfume of mountain blossoms.

Their journey: a sturdy rope ferry, mossy ropes groaning, Bunting nestled in her satchel, nose peeking. Down, down into a vast echoing crater already in full roar. Laughter. Brass trumpets. Distant majestic dragon-roars that shook the soles of Morwen’s boots. Banners of swirling dragons and soaring birds.

Near the grand viewing platform they met a young dragon. Magnificent, of course: scales like polished emeralds, eyes the colour of a summer sky, wide with a nervous sheen. What caught Morwen was his posture. Wings tucked so neatly, tail coiled with such precision, he looked less like a fearsome beast than a particularly well-behaved gentleman waiting for afternoon tea. Claws tucked away. Long neck at an angle of polite inquiry.

“Good day, esteemed judge,” he said, a smooth rumble, distant thunder asked to keep its volume down. “I am Aerion. It is an honour to be considered, though I do hope my presentation meets with your approval.”

Morwen noticed the faint tremor in his wings. “And to you, Aerion. Are you preparing for your performance? You seem remarkably poised.”

Aerion’s head dipped, profound solemnity. “I endeavour to present my most graceful aerial ballet. Though I confess the pressure is considerable. My cousin, Ignis, has already performed a rather dazzling array of fiery loops. His breath control is, frankly, astonishing. He managed to roast an entire pig in mid-air with a single well-aimed blast. Quite the spectacle.”

Morwen heard the anxious tremor beneath the polish, a heart more sensitive than the frame suggested. Dragon stage fright: a whirlwind of worried thoughts and fluttering scales.

The festival commenced with more noise than Mount Glimmer usually allowed before breakfast. A griffon performed a rather showy, ultimately predictable dive-bombing routine, feathers ruffled by the wind. Then came the dragons. There were dragons who juggled glowing embers with surprising dexterity, dragons who carved intricate fleeting patterns in the air with streams of perfumed smoke, and dragons who sang songs so loud they made the mountains vibrate, causing a cascade of small pebbles to tumble down the crater walls. Morwen took notes she would later pretend were more official than they were. Bunting took notes with his nose.

Ignis took the sky. Raw power, magnificent spectacle. He spun, dipped, let loose a torrent of golden flame that coalesced into a roaring lion, fiery mane writhing. The crowd erupted. Morwen, impressed, noted the sheer volume and ferocity.

Aerion, perched on the platform edge, visibly deflated. Emerald scales dimmed. Perfect posture slumped. A small mournful huff that smelled of disappointment and dew-kissed roses, a surprisingly delicate scent. Without a word he launched himself, ungracefully for him, and disappeared into the misty heights, a streak of fading green.

“Well now.” Morwen’s brow furrowed like a ploughed field. “Ignis’s fiery display has rather extinguished young Aerion’s spirit.”

Bunting nudged the satchel, hopped out with a determined air, and waddled toward the direction Aerion had flown, little legs a blur.

“Bunting, where are you going?” The marmot’s sniff said this was important. Morwen followed, sensible boots on gravel.

They found Aerion huddled on a lonely wind-swept ledge, magnificent wings wrapped around him as if for protection from an unseen chill. Thoroughly dejected, usually bright eyes downcast, reflecting the grey swirling mist. Bunting, without a moment’s hesitation, trotted right up to the dragon’s colossal snout, tiny form a stark contrast, and offered a plump glistening mountain berry, skin a deep inviting purple. The wind tried to steal it. Bunting did not allow this.

Aerion blinked. Sniffed cautiously. “I don’t think I can,” he whispered, thick. “My performance was inadequate. Ignis was so magnificent. I am simply not cut from the same fiery cloth.”

Bunting nudged the berry again, then sat up and began to groom his whiskers with meticulous care, unbothered. A small anchor in the vastness of Aerion’s sorrow.

Aerion watched. No expectation. No judgment. Simple being. Hesitantly he plucked the berry with massive claws, surprising gentleness. Sweet and cool, a burst that cut through despair. He ate it, then another.

“You see, Aerion,” Morwen said, joining them, voice like a soft breeze, “it is not always about the loudest roar or the brightest flame.” She did not hand him a shopping list of virtues. She sat. Bunting munched. The mist moved as mist does.

Aerion looked at Morwen, then at Bunting, tail giving a contented twitch. He spread his wings, not in a grand fiery display, but with a slow graceful unfurling, like the opening of a magnificent bloom. He dipped his head.

“Perhaps my sky-dance is not meant to be a competition. Perhaps it is meant to be a feeling. A whisper in the wind, rather than a shout from the mountaintops.”

Then he began to move. Not Ignis’s explosive power: a breathtaking fluid elegance entirely his own. He did not breathe fire. He traced ribbons of shimmering moonlight, pearlescent trails that hung a moment before fading. He danced with the mist, weaving like a gentle current, quiet joy, a profound peace settling over the lonely ledge. Not a performance to be judged. A gift to be witnessed.

The crowd, beginning to disperse, heard the ethereal music of his flight and looked up. Stunned silence. The young dragon painted the sky. Morwen gave a discreet nod, eyes crinkling. Bunting, on her shoulder, sighed, a soft rumbling satisfaction.

As the sun dipped below the peaks, casting long purple shadows across the crater, the festival culminated not in a grand pronouncement from the judges but in a quiet shared understanding that rippled through villagers and dragons. They gathered. They shared roasted mountain roots, steaming mugs of elderflower cordial, and stories, roars now softened to companionable rumbling. Ignis, for all his fiery brilliance, even offered Aerion a shy nod of respect, a silent acknowledgment of a different yet equally valid kind of power. He even tried a delicate aerial loop himself, and only managed to sneeze a puff of smoke that smelled suspiciously of burnt toast.

Morwen watched the cozy scene unfold in the warm glow of a hundred lanterns, a well-tended garden finally in bloom, and did not quote the old ones about small hearts and high soaring. Aerion’s moonlight ribbons faded. Bunting found another berry. The bells in the hidden valleys, for once, sounded as if they had been listening.
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
